q: How many bank accounts can a resident individual investor register with a mutual fund folio?
e: A resident individual investor can register up to 5 bank accounts per folio. One must be designated as the default for redemption proceeds.

q: Maximum number of nominees that can be registered in a mutual fund folio is:
e: A folio can have up to 3 nominees, with allocation percentages aggregating to 100%.

q: Investors have the right to specify up to ___ investment folios as part of nomination requirements.
e: The maximum permissible nominees in a folio is three.

q: KYC for mutual fund investors is performed by:
e: KYC is centralized via SEBI-registered KRAs (CAMS-KRA, KFin-KRA, etc.). Once done, valid across all SEBI intermediaries.

q: Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) is sent to the investor:
o: Monthly (if any transaction) and half-yearly otherwise
e: CAS is sent monthly when transactions occur, and half-yearly even with no transactions. Consolidated across all folios using PAN.

q: The minimum subscription amount for SIP can be as low as:
e: SEBI permits SIPs starting from ₹100 (some AMCs allow ₹100, most start at ₹500). Recent push for ₹250 SIPs to drive financial inclusion.

q: In what form do mutual fund distributors earn revenue?
o: Commission from mutual funds for distribution
e: Distributors earn commission from the mutual fund (AMC). They cannot charge investors directly. Trail commission accrues over time the investor stays invested.

q: Transmission in a mutual fund refers to:
o: Transfer of units to nominees/legal heirs on death of unitholder
e: Transmission = transfer of units to nominee/legal heir upon death of unitholder. Different from transfer (which is voluntary).

q: Which of the following is NOT mandatory for investing in a mutual fund?
e: Nomination is now mandatory or requires opt-out. PAN, KYC, and bank account are mandatory. (Note: SEBI has made nomination effectively mandatory via opt-in/opt-out.)

q: In a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP), the investor:
o: Pays the AMC a regular fee
e: SWP allows investors to withdraw a pre-specified amount at regular intervals — useful for retirement income planning.

q: Cooling-off / Right of Refusal applies in:
o: Mis-sold products only as per investor charter
e: Investor charter and grievance mechanisms allow recourse for mis-selling. Mutual funds don't have a blanket cooling-off period like insurance.

q: Switching from a regular plan to a direct plan within the same scheme:
o: Is treated as redemption + fresh subscription for tax/exit load
e: Switch from regular to direct (or any switch) is treated as a redemption from one and subscription to another — taxable event and may attract exit load.

q: Maximum nominees in a folio:
e: Up to 3 nominees, allocation must total 100%.

q: Maximum bank accounts a resident individual can register in a folio:
e: Up to 5 bank accounts per folio.

q: Distributors earn revenue in the form of:
e: Commission from MFs for distribution.

q: CAS is sent:
e: Monthly when transactions occur, half-yearly otherwise.

q: KYC is performed by:
e: Centralized via SEBI-registered KRAs.

q: KYC compliance is mandatory for:
o: All investors regardless of investment value
e: All investors — individual and non-individual, including joint holders, NRIs, PoA holders, guardians of minors — must be KYC compliant regardless of investment value.

q: PAN is mandatory for mutual fund investments EXCEPT for:
o: Investments up to ₹50,000 per investor per year per MF
e: PAN-exempt: investments (lump-sum + SIP combined) up to ₹50,000 per investor per year per mutual fund. Also: officials of govt./court, Sikkim residents, certain UN entities.

q: For Micro-SIPs (PAN-exempt), the investor is issued a:
e: Investors using PAN exemption receive a PEKRN (PAN Exempt KYC Reference Number) from the KRA, quoted on the application form along with photo-ID.

q: The benefit of the centralised KYC process via KRAs is that:
o: Each AMC must do its own KYC
Once KYC is done with one capital market intermediary, it is valid across the capital market
KYC must be redone every year
e: KRAs centralise KYC across the capital market. Once done with one SEBI intermediary (broker, MF, depository participant), the investor can transact across the market without repeating KYC.

q: CERSAI was authorised by the Government of India to function as the:
o: Central KYC Records Registry (cKYCR) under PML Rules
e: Government of India (Nov 2015 notification) authorised CERSAI to act as the Central KYC Records Registry under Prevention of Money Laundering Rules.

q: In-Person Verification (IPV) of an investor must be done:
o: By the capital market intermediary as part of the KYC process
e: IPV is mandatory: the SEBI-registered intermediary must verify the investor in person before uploading data to KRA. Confirms identity and prevents impersonation.

q: The maximum period for an NFO of a non-ELSS open-ended scheme is:
e: NFO of a non-ELSS open-ended scheme can be open for a maximum of 15 days. ELSS schemes can have up to 30-day NFOs.

q: After NFO closure, an open-ended scheme must reopen for ongoing sale and repurchase within:
e: Open-ended schemes must reopen for sale/repurchase within 5 business days from the closure of the NFO.

q: A distributor must obtain which credential before distributing mutual funds?
o: ARN from AMFI after passing NISM V-A and KYD
e: A distributor must pass NISM V-A, complete KYD (Know Your Distributor), and obtain ARN from AMFI before distributing mutual fund schemes.

q: The EUIN of the relationship manager is captured on the application form to:
o: Track the specific individual employee who advised the investor
e: EUIN identifies the individual employee/RM within the ARN-holder firm who advised the investor — protects against future "execution-only" mis-selling claims and ensures accountability.

q: The body that has been authorised to act as Central KYC Records Registry (cKYCR) is:
e: CERSAI was authorised by the Government of India (Nov 2015) to act as cKYCR under Prevention of Money Laundering Rules.

q: For mutual fund investments up to which limit per investor per year per MF, PAN is not mandatory?
e: PAN-exempt limit is ₹50,000 per investor per year per mutual fund (combined limit for SIPs and lump-sum).

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid alternative photo-ID for PAN-exempt investors?
e: Credit card is excluded since it may not be backed by a bank account. Voter ID, Driving License, Passport, Aadhaar etc. are valid.

q: Maximum NFO period for an ELSS scheme:
e: ELSS NFOs can be open up to 30 days. Other open-ended schemes are capped at 15 days.

q: The maximum number of nominees that can be specified in a mutual fund folio is:
e: A folio can have up to 3 nominees. Allocation percentages must aggregate to 100%.

q: Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) is sent to investors:
e: CAS is sent monthly when there is any transaction in any folio (across MFs by PAN), and half-yearly even when no transaction occurs.

q: A Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) involves:
o: Transferring a fixed amount from one scheme to another at specified intervals
e: STP transfers fixed amounts from one scheme to another at regular intervals — typically debt → equity for systematic deployment of lump sums.

q: The minimum investment for SIP in a mutual fund scheme can be as low as:
e: SEBI / AMFI permit small-ticket SIPs; some AMCs allow SIPs starting ₹250-₹500 to drive financial inclusion.

q: Whose KYC must be completed in case of an application by a minor?
o: Any family member of the minor
e: For minor investors, the GUARDIAN must be KYC compliant. Once the minor turns 18, they must complete their own KYC and update the folio status.

q: Investors have the right to specify up to ___ nominees for their mutual fund investment folios.
e: Investors can specify up to 3 nominees per folio. Allocation percentages must aggregate to 100%.

q: Trail commission on a SIP of ₹10,000/month at 0.5% p.a. trail, for an investor who has held for 1 year (approx avg AUM ₹65,000). Approx annual trail to distributor is:
e: Trail = 0.5% × ₹65,000 (approx avg AUM) ≈ ₹325. Trail is small per-investor but recurring & sticky.

q: Deployment of funds collected during NFO must follow timelines mentioned in:
e: Per Regulation 35(5), AMCs must specify realistic deployment timelines in the SID. Failure to deploy as committed may attract regulatory action.

q: Allotment of units (or refund) for an NFO must be done within:
e: Units must be allotted (or refunds processed) within 5 business days of NFO closure. Open-ended schemes must reopen within 5 business days too.

q: NRIs (Non-Resident Indians) are eligible to invest in Indian mutual fund schemes:
o: Yes, on repatriable or non-repatriable basis as per FEMA
e: NRIs can invest in Indian MFs, on repatriable or non-repatriable basis, complying with FEMA rules. They use NRE/NRO accounts. KYC and FATCA requirements apply.

q: Overseas Corporate Bodies (OCBs) are __ to invest in Indian mutual funds:
e: OCBs are NOT permitted to invest in Indian mutual fund schemes (per RBI/FEMA rules; OCB category was de-recognised long ago).

q: Foreign citizens (non-NRIs, non-FPIs) residing outside India are __ to invest in Indian mutual funds:
o: Generally NOT permitted (only specific FPI/QFI routes available)
e: Foreign citizens cannot directly invest in Indian MFs. They must route via FPI registration or QFI scheme. Mutual funds can permit them only as per regulatory carve-outs.

q: Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) wishing to invest in mutual funds:
o: Can invest, with the Karta acting on behalf of the HUF and HUF PAN used
Can invest only in liquid funds
e: HUFs can invest in MFs. Karta operates the folio on behalf of the HUF. HUF PAN is used. KYC of the Karta is required.

q: A minor investor in mutual funds — when the minor turns 18:
o: Status is changed to "major" by submitting prescribed documents (PAN, KYC, signature, bank account)
e: On attaining majority, the investor must submit prescribed documents (PAN, fresh KYC, signature attestation, bank account) to convert the folio from "minor" to "major". The guardian's rights cease.

q: Power of Attorney (PoA) holders for mutual fund investments must:
o: Be KYC-compliant themselves AND have the PoA document on record
e: PoA holders must complete KYC themselves AND register the notarised PoA document. Both KYC and PoA are needed before transactions on behalf of the actual investor.

q: When an investor in a Pay-out option of IDCW elects to switch to Re-investment of IDCW:
o: Re-investment option overrides — going forward, dividends are reinvested as additional units
e: When investor switches IDCW option, the new election overrides. Going forward, dividends are reinvested at ex-dividend NAV (Re-investment) instead of being paid out (Pay-out).

q: Time stamping of mutual fund transactions is done at:
o: Official Points of Acceptance (OPoAs) registered with the AMC
e: Time stamping is at OPoAs (Official Points of Acceptance), which include AMC offices, RTA offices, designated branches. Cut-off time is determined by OPoA receipt time.

q: A distributor accepting an application from an investor must forward it to the OPoA:
o: At the earliest possible — cut-off time is determined by OPoA receipt
e: Distributor receipt is NOT cut-off-relevant. The OPoA receipt time is. Distributor must forward applications quickly to ensure investor's intended cut-off is met.

q: NACH (National Automated Clearing House) is used in mutual funds for:
o: Auto-debit of SIP installments from investor's bank account
e: NACH mandate authorises the AMC/RTA to debit the investor's bank account on SIP dates automatically. Standardised under NPCI.

q: Standing Instruction (SI) for SIPs is set up via:
o: The investor's bank, instructing periodic transfer to the scheme
e: Standing Instructions are bank-level periodic transfer mandates. Alternative to NACH; fewer banks support modern SI but it's available.

q: In a Micro-SIP (annual investment ≤ ₹50,000), the investor uses:
o: PEKRN (PAN Exempt KYC Reference Number) + alternative photo-ID
e: Micro-SIPs are PAN-exempt up to ₹50,000/year per MF. Investor uses PEKRN + alternative photo-ID (Voter, DL, Passport etc.). Cumulative limit applies.

q: e-KYC via UIDAI (Aadhaar OTP-based) for mutual fund accounts is permitted with limits — the investment cap on accounts opened through OTP-based e-KYC is typically:
e: OTP-based e-KYC has a per-investor annual investment cap (₹50,000 aggregate) due to lighter verification. Full biometric e-KYC or in-person KYC removes this cap.

q: CKYC (Central KYC Records Registry) and KRA-KYC are:
o: Different — CKYC is wider (whole financial sector via CERSAI), KRA-KYC is securities-market specific
e: CKYC: cross-sector (CERSAI under PML Rules), covers all financial services. KRA: SEBI-registered, securities-market-specific. Both aim to centralise KYC; complementary.

q: MITRA (Mutual Fund Investment Tracing and Retrieval Assistant) is hosted by:
o: Two Qualified RTAs — CAMS and KFin Technologies
e: MITRA is hosted by CAMS and KFin (the two QRTAs). Allows investors to trace inactive/unclaimed folios across the industry. Reduces unclaimed assets.

q: A "dormant" or inactive folio is one where:
o: No financial transaction has occurred for a specified period
e: Dormant folio = no financial transactions for a specified period (varies, typically 1-2 years for monitoring; longer for true inactivity). Triggers re-verification of KYC and contact details.

q: Voluntary lock-in / debit freeze on a mutual fund folio (recently introduced by SEBI) is:
o: Optional — investor can lock units to prevent unauthorised redemption
e: SEBI introduced voluntary debit freeze (March 2026 circular) — investors can voluntarily lock units to prevent unauthorised redemption. Available across demat and SoA folios via MF Central.

q: Transmission of units (in case of unitholder's demise) requires the nominee/legal heir to submit:
o: Death certificate, KYC of claimant, transmission request, may need succession proof if no nominee
e: Transmission docs: death certificate, KYC of nominee/legal heir, transmission request form. If no nominee, succession certificate or probate is required (which is much harder).

q: A nomination on a mutual fund folio:
o: Can be changed at any time by the unitholder by submitting a fresh nomination form
e: Unitholder can change nomination anytime via fresh nomination form. New nomination overrides earlier. No consent of existing nominee needed (it's the unitholder's right).

q: CKYC and KRA-KYC differ in that:
o: CKYC is wider (whole financial sector via CERSAI), KRA-KYC is securities-market specific
e: CKYC: cross-financial-sector (CERSAI under PML Rules). KRA: SEBI-registered, securities-market only. Complementary systems.

q: MITRA (the unclaimed-mutual-fund-folio platform) is run by:
o: CAMS and KFin (the two QRTAs) as agents of AMCs
e: MITRA is hosted by CAMS and KFin (two Qualified RTAs) as agents of AMCs. Helps trace inactive/unclaimed mutual fund folios.

q: A new SEBI rule (March 2026) introduced a "voluntary debit freeze" facility — its purpose is to:
o: Allow investors to lock units against unauthorised redemption
e: Voluntary lock-in / debit freeze allows investors to proactively lock units to prevent unauthorised redemption. Available via MF Central platform across demat and SoA folios.

q: Foreign citizens (non-NRI, non-FPI, non-QFI) — direct investment in Indian mutual funds is:
o: Generally NOT permitted (must route via specific FPI/QFI routes)
e: Direct foreign citizen investment in Indian MFs is generally not permitted. They must route via FPI registration or QFI scheme.

q: The maximum number of nominees in a mutual fund folio is:
e: Up to 3 nominees per folio, with allocation percentages summing to 100%.

q: NRIs (Non-Resident Indians) wishing to invest in Indian MFs:
o: Can invest on repatriable / non-repatriable basis under FEMA, using NRE/NRO accounts; KYC + FATCA required
e: NRIs can invest in Indian MFs under FEMA, using NRE (repatriable) or NRO (non-repatriable) accounts. KYC + FATCA compliance is mandatory.

q: In a Mutual Fund SIP — the benefit of Rupee Cost Averaging is that:
o: Investor buys more units when NAV is low and fewer when NAV is high — averaging cost downward
e: Rupee cost averaging: fixed amount buys more units at low NAV, fewer at high NAV. Average cost typically lower than simple average of NAVs.
